claims.claim: Scenarios with constant fitness landscapes are not generic and should be the exception rather than the norm.
claims.source: Thus, while scenarios with constant fitness landscapes are a special case of the general birth-death process that describes evolution, such scenarios are not generic, and instead should be the exception rather than the norm.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the complexity of birth-death processes.

claims.claim: An evolutionary birth-death process is a complex dynamical system.
claims.source: Generally speaking, an evolutionary birth-death process is a complex dynamical system, and there is no reason to expect that there exists a function that can describe the dynamics of such a complex system so that the function increases along trajectories in the state space of the system.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on dynamical systems theory.

claims.claim: A Lyapunov function is a function that increases along trajectories in the state space of a dynamical system.
claims.source: In dynamical systems theory, such a function is sometimes called a Lyapunov function (Devaney, 1986), and it is well known that most dynamical systems do not have a Lyapunov function, essentially because their dynamics are too complicated.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from dynamical systems theory, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Most dynamical systems do not have a Lyapunov function because their dynamics are too complicated.
claims.source: In dynamical systems theory, such a function is sometimes called a Lyapunov function (Devaney, 1986), and it is well known that most dynamical systems do not have a Lyapunov function, essentially because their dynamics are too complicated.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from dynamical systems theory.

claims.claim: A global, time-independent fitness function would be equivalent to a Lyapunov function for evolutionary dynamics.
claims.source: But a Lyapunov function is exactly what a global, time-independent fitness function would amount to: a function in type space that predicts evolutionary trajectories in the sense that the function increases along evolutionary trajectories, so that the eventual outcome of evolution is a maximum of that function.
claims.evidence: This is an inference connecting concepts from dynamical systems theory to evolutionary biology.

claims.claim: For general evolutionary birth-death processes, there is no fitness function that would predict their outcome.
claims.source: It follows that for general evolutionary birth-death processes, there is no fitness function that would predict their outcome.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the previous arguments about Lyapunov functions.

claims.claim: Fitness is a derived property of evolutionary systems, not a basic ingredient.
claims.source: But even in that case it is important to realize that the fitness function would be a derived property of the system, and not a basic ingredient.
claims.evidence: This is a central theoretical claim of the manuscript.

claims.claim: The basic ingredients of an evolving system are birth and death rates and the offspring function, not fitness.
claims.source: The basic ingredients of an evolving system are birth and death rates (and the offspring function), and not "fitness".
claims.evidence: This is a central theoretical claim of the manuscript.

claims.claim: Starting evolutionary theory based on the notion of fitness represents an unjustified argumentative leap.
claims.source: Starting an evolutionary theory based on the notion of fitness thus represents an argumentative leap that is unjustified a priori.
claims.evidence: This is a critical inference about the foundations of evolutionary theory.

claims.claim: Evolutionary game theory is generally based on fitness functions in the form of payoff matrices.
claims.source: Incidentally, this also applies to evolutionary game theory (Hofbauer and Sigmund, 1998; Maynard Smith, 1982) and its extensions (Brown, 2016), which are generally also based on fitness functions, e.g. in the form of payoff matrices.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of evolutionary game theory supported by citations.

claims.claim: Evolutionary game theory has generated important insights into frequency-dependent selection and social evolution.
claims.source: Evolutionary game theory is a powerful tool that has generated many important and fundamental insights into processes of frequency-dependent selection, e.g. in the context of social evolution (Sigmund, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the field supported by citation.

claims.claim: Most game theoretic models have the limitation that they are based on ad hoc fitness functions not derived from underlying birth-death processes.
claims.source: Nevertheless, most game theoretic models have the limitation that they are based on ad hoc fitness functions, which are usually not derived from underlying birth-death processes (for an exception see e.g. Traulsen et al. (2005) and Huang et al. (2015), who derive deterministic game dynamics from underlying stochastic processes in finite populations).
claims.evidence: This is a critical assessment of the field with citations to exceptions.

claims.claim: The mathematical theory of stochastic processes is well developed.
claims.source: The mathematical theory of stochastic processes is well developed (see e.g. Karlin and Taylor (1975) for an introduction), but complete mathematical tractability is only possible for relatively simple birth-death processes.
claims.evidence: This is established mathematical knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Complete mathematical tractability is only possible for relatively simple birth-death processes.
claims.source: The mathematical theory of stochastic processes is well developed (see e.g. Karlin and Taylor (1975) for an introduction), but complete mathematical tractability is only possible for relatively simple birth-death processes.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about mathematical limitations.

claims.claim: Any evolutionary birth-death process can be described by a differential Master equation.
claims.source: In principle, any evolutionary birth-death process can be described by a differential Master equation for the probability of an evolving system to have a given number of individuals of each type at a given moment in time (Van Kampen, 1992).
claims.evidence: This is established mathematical knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Master equations can only be solved analytically for simple model scenarios.
claims.source: However, such equations can only be solved analytically for simple model scenarios, e.g. when birth and death rates are constant and the offspring function is very simple.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about mathematical limitations.

claims.claim: Under certain conditions, in the limit of large populations, evolutionary birth-death processes can be described by partial differential equations.
claims.source: For example, Nicholas Champagnat and colleagues (Champagnat et al., 2006, 2008) have shown that under certain conditions, in the limit of large populations evolutionary birth-death processes can be described by partial differential equations.
claims.evidence: This is a mathematical result supported by citations.

claims.claim: The type of analytical approximation obtained depends on the type of limits taken.
claims.source: One interesting result is that the type of analytical approximation one obtains depends very much on the type of limits one takes (Champagnat et al., 2006; Dieckmann and Law, 1996).
claims.evidence: This is a mathematical result supported by citations.

claims.claim: Different approximations can describe the same evolutionary birth-death process.
claims.source: Thus, different approximations can describe the same evolutionary birth-death process, and the question then becomes which one of these approximations is biologically most relevant.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the relationship between mathematical approximations and biological reality.

claims.claim: The canonical equation of adaptive dynamics (Equation 3) describes the dynamics of mean type under assumptions of large populations and rare, small mutations.
claims.source: An interesting approximation is obtained by assuming not only that population sizes are large, but also that beneficial mutations are exceedingly rare and small (this is only a rough description, as the details of what "rare" and "small" means are important, see Champagnat et al. (2006), Dieckmann and Law (1996)). In that case, the dynamics of the mean type x¯ of an evolving population is given by a differential equation(3)dx¯dt∝∂f(x¯,y)∂y|y=x¯.
claims.evidence: This is a mathematical result from adaptive dynamics theory supported by citations.

claims.claim: Equation 3 is an example of the canonical equation of adaptive dynamics.
claims.source: Equation 3 is an example of the so-called canonical equation of adaptive dynamics (Dieckmann and Law, 1996), which is the theoretical framework for the analysis of evolutionary dynamics derived from invasion fitness functions (Diekmann, 2004; Geritz et al., 1998; Metz et al., 1992, 1996).
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of the equation supported by citations to adaptive dynamics literature.

claims.claim: Figure 1 illustrates the approximation obtained from adaptive dynamics for the evolutionary birth-death processes shown in Videos 1 and 2.
claims.source: Figure 1 illustrates the approximation obtained from the adaptive dynamics (Equation 3) for the evolutionary birth-death processes shown in Video 1 and Video 2.
claims.evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Invasion fitness can be derived from evolutionary birth-death processes as a general principle.
claims.source: Invasion fitness can be derived from evolutionary birth-death processes not only for particular cases, but as a general principle (Dieckmann and Law, 1996), and adaptive dynamics can therefore be used to gain general insights into such processes.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citation.

claims.claim: The fitness landscape defined by invasion fitness is generally not constant because it depends on the current biotic environment.
claims.source: However, there is a fundamental difference between invasion fitness and the traditional concept of constant fitness landscapes (apart from the fact that the latter are generally not derived from evolutionary birth-death processes). The difference is that the landscape defined by invasion fitness is generally not constant: because the landscape is a function of the current biotic environment, i.e., of the current resident types, it changes as the population evolves.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the properties of invasion fitness.

claims.claim: Invasion fitness defines a dynamical system on fitness landscapes.
claims.source: In essence, invasion fitness defines a dynamical system on fitness landscapes.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical characterization of invasion fitness.

claims.claim: Populations can evolve to occupy fitness minima even though always evolving uphill on a changing fitness landscape.
claims.source: A paradigmatic example of the dynamics of fitness landscapes occurs when populations, even though always evolving 'uphill' on a changing fitness landscape, eventually come to occupy a fitness minimum. This sounds like an oxymoron, but is in fact a generic and robust outcome of the dynamics of fitness landscapes (Geritz et al., 1998)
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical result from adaptive dynamics supported by citation.

claims.claim: Evolutionary branching is often the consequence of convergence to fitness minima.
claims.source: The related phenomenon of evolutionary branching, which is often the consequence of convergence to such fitness minima, has been studied extensively in the context of the important problem of adaptive diversification and speciation (Dieckmann et al., 2004; Doebeli, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a claim about evolutionary branching supported by citations.

claims.claim: Birth-death processes are fundamentally ecological because they result in temporal fluctuations in population size.
claims.source: Birth-death processes are fundamentally ecological, because they result in temporal fluctuations in the number of individuals in the population.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the ecological nature of birth-death processes.

claims.claim: There is no fundamental difference between ecological and evolutionary birth-death processes, and hence between ecological and evolutionary dynamics.
claims.source: Formally, there is thus no fundamental difference between ecological and evolutionary birth-death processes, and hence between ecological and evolutionary dynamics.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the unity of ecological and evolutionary processes.

claims.claim: The difference between ecology and evolution becomes one of time scales when the offspring function is close to the identity.
claims.source: The difference between ecology and evolution then becomes one of time scales. On shorter time scales, evolutionary innovation is negligible, and hence the birth-death process is mainly ecological, while on longer time scales exploration of larger areas of type space is possible, and evolutionary change becomes important.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about time scale separation in evolutionary processes.

claims.claim: Invasion fitness is an intrinsically ecological quantity defined as the growth rate of a mutant in a resident population undergoing ecological dynamics.
claims.source: For example, the concept of invasion fitness discussed in the previous section is based on the distinction between ecological and evolutionary time scales. Invasion fitness is an intrinsically ecological quantity, because it is defined as the (ecological) growth rate of a mutant type occurring in a resident population undergoing purely ecological dynamics.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical characterization of invasion fitness.

claims.claim: Separation of ecological and evolutionary time scales essentially reflects an approximation of the underlying evolutionary birth-death process.
claims.source: Separation of ecological and evolutionary time scales essentially reflects an approximation of the underlying evolutionary birth-death process, and invasion fitness provides the hinge for connecting ecological to evolutionary dynamics.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the nature of time scale separation.

claims.claim: Separation of ecological and evolutionary time scales may not always be a good approximation when evolutionary innovations are large and frequent.
claims.source: It must be kept in mind, however, that separation of ecological and evolutionary time scales may not always be a good approximation of evolutionary birth-death processes, because evolutionary innovations may be large and frequent rather than gradual and rare (e.g. in microbes).
claims.evidence: This is a caveat about the applicability of time scale separation, with microbes given as an example.

claims.claim: When evolutionary innovations are large and frequent, a clear distinction between ecological and evolutionary processes becomes impossible.
claims.source: In such scenarios, a clear distinction between ecological and evolutionary processes becomes impossible.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about scenarios where time scale separation breaks down.

claims.claim: There has been much discussion about how to model social evolution and what fitness measures should be employed.
claims.source: There has been much discussion in recent years about how to model social evolution, and about what the correct "fitness measures" are that should be employed in such models (e.g. the paper Nowak et al. (2010) elicited a response with 137 signatories).
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of debates in the field supported by citation.

claims.claim: Some researchers have suggested that inclusive fitness is necessary for understanding social evolution.
claims.source: Some researchers have suggested that considering "inclusive fitness", a fitness measure that takes into account an individual's own fitness as well as that of its relatives (Hamilton, 1964), is necessary for understanding social evolution, and that inclusive fitness is the quantity that is maximized in Darwinian evolution in general (Grafen, 2007, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of a position in the field supported by citations.

claims.claim: Hamilton introduced the concept of inclusive fitness in 1964.
claims.source: Some researchers have suggested that considering "inclusive fitness", a fitness measure that takes into account an individual's own fitness as well as that of its relatives (Hamilton, 1964), is necessary for understanding social evolution
claims.evidence: This is a historical citation to the origin of inclusive fitness.

claims.claim: Social evolution must be the consequence of some evolutionary birth-death process.
claims.source: However, like any other evolutionary phenomenon, social evolution must be the consequence of some evolutionary birth-death process, and because of their potential complexity (particularly in the context of social interactions), such processes do not in general admit a global fitness function from which their dynamics can be derived.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim applying the birth-death framework to social evolution.

claims.claim: In existing models of social evolution, inclusive fitness is almost never derived from an underlying birth-death process.
claims.source: In existing models of social evolution, inclusive fitness is almost never derived from an underlying birth-death process, and deriving an inclusive fitness function capturing the dynamics of the underlying process would only be possible under special assumptions.
claims.evidence: This is a critical observation about current modeling practices in social evolution.

claims.claim: In a birth-death process for social evolution, individuals do not 'know' anything about maximizing inclusive fitness.
claims.source: In a birth-death process for social evolution, individuals obviously do not "know" anything about maximizing inclusive fitness.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the mechanistic nature of birth-death processes.

claims.claim: Birth and death rates of each individual are calculated independently of the degree of relatedness of other individuals.
claims.source: Instead, individuals characterized by certain social traits simply give birth and die at certain rates, which are determined independently for each individual. Birth rates (and death rates) of different individuals may of course be correlated, e.g. due to a shared environment, but birth and death rates of each individual are calculated independently, and, in particular, independently of the degree of relatedness of other individuals.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about how birth-death processes work in social evolution.

claims.claim: Social evolution is an emergent property of the birth-death process.
claims.source: Social evolution is then an emergent property of this process.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the nature of social evolution in the birth-death framework.

claims.claim: In some scenarios it may be possible to describe emergent social dynamics using an inclusive fitness measure, but such a measure would be derived from the birth-death process, not a basic ingredient.
claims.source: In some scenarios it may be possible to subsume and describe the emergent dynamics using an inclusive fitness measure, but such a fitness measure would not be a basic ingredient of the underlying birth-death process, and instead could at best be a quantity that is derived from that process.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the status of inclusive fitness in the birth-death framework.

claims.claim: If it is possible to derive inclusive fitness, then it is also possible to derive other fitness measures such as direct fitness.
claims.source: Moreover, if it is possible to derive this quantity, then it is also possible to derive other fitness measures that would describe the dynamics of the process, such as the direct fitness measures used in evolutionary game theory. Direct fitness measures simply calculate the average number of offspring per unit time of the different cooperative types, taking into account the expected cooperative environment of each type, i.e., the degree of positive assortment between cooperating individuals (Fletcher and Doebeli, 2009; Nathanson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about alternative fitness measures supported by citations.

claims.claim: Many processes of social evolution may be too complicated to admit any fitness measure from which their dynamics could be derived.
claims.source: In reality, many processes of social evolution, e.g. in the microbial world, may be too complicated to readily admit any sort of fitness measure from which their dynamics could be derived.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about the complexity of real social evolution processes.

claims.claim: The birth-death perspective reveals that there is no fitness concept fundamentally necessary for understanding social evolution.
claims.source: Thus, the perspective of evolutionary birth-death processes reveals that there is no fitness concept that would be fundamentally necessary for understanding social evolution.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion about social evolution in the birth-death framework.

claims.claim: It has been argued that social evolution should be investigated in the context of multi-level selection.
claims.source: It has been argued that it is often useful to investigate social evolution in the context of group selection, i.e., of multi-level selection scenarios in which fitness accrues to both individuals and groups of individuals (Wilson and Wilson, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of a position in the field supported by citation.

claims.claim: The Price equation is the main theoretical tool for investigating multi-level selection.
claims.source: Somewhat curiously, the main theoretical tool for such investigations is the Price equation (Price, 1970).
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the field supported by citation.

claims.claim: The Price equation is not really a model but a useful data visualization tool that takes stock of what happened over one generation.
claims.source: On the one hand, the Price equation is not really a model, but a useful data visualization tool: it takes stock of what happened over one parent-offspring generation (Price, 1970; van Veelen et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of the Price equation supported by citations.

claims.claim: The Price equation takes place at the level of individual organisms and does not describe multi-level processes.
claims.source: On the other hand, this accounting takes place at the level of individual organisms, and hence, again by construction, the Price equation does not describe multi-level processes.
claims.evidence: This is a critical inference about the limitations of the Price equation.

claims.claim: Individual-level selection requires individual-level events, i.e., individuals undergoing a birth-death process.
claims.source: In other words, in the perspective of evolutionary birth-death processes, individual-level selection requires individual-level events, i.e., individuals undergoing a birth-death process.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical definition of individual-level selection in the birth-death framework.

claims.claim: Processes of group selection require group level events such as group fission and extinction.
claims.source: Generalizing from this, processes of group selection require group level events. For example, groups could fission into smaller groups at certain rates, and groups could go extinct, which would define a birth-death process at the the level of groups.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical definition of group selection in the birth-death framework.

claims.claim: Multi-level selection requires a birth-death process at multiple levels of biological organization.
claims.source: More generally, multi-level selection requires a birth-death process at multiple levels of biological organization.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical definition of multi-level selection in the birth-death framework.

claims.claim: Simon et al. (2013) introduced evolutionary birth-death processes that unfold at both individual and group levels.
claims.source: In Simon et al. (2013) we have introduced evolutionary birth-death processes that unfold at both the individual and the group levels, and we have given examples of social evolution where the social traits are only maintained in the population because of group level events
claims.evidence: This is a citation to the authors' previous work.

claims.claim: It is only appropriate to say a social trait evolves by group selection when the trait is maintained because of group level events.
claims.source: We would argue that only in such situations is it appropriate to say that a social trait evolves by group selection (Simon et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the definition of group selection supported by citation.

claims.claim: To talk about selection at a certain level of biological organization, one needs to formulate an evolutionary birth-death process at that level.
claims.source: In general, to talk about selection at a certain level of biological organization, one needs to formulate an evolutionary birth-death process at that level.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical principle about defining selection at different levels.

claims.claim: Evolution of cooperation due to spatial clustering is not due to group selection but to individual selection in structured environments.
claims.source: This is of course not always possible, e.g. when cooperation evolves in spatially structured populations due to clustering of cooperators, in which case it is often not feasible to identify the clusters as reproductive units due to their ephemeral nature. In that sense, evolution of cooperation due to spatial clustering is not due to group selection, but rather to individual selection in structured environments (leading to assortment of cooperators).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the nature of selection in spatially structured populations.

claims.claim: Group selection may be an important driver for the evolution of eusociality.
claims.source: In particular, group selection may be an important driver for the evolution of eusociality (Nowak et al., 2010; Shaffer et al., 2016; Wilson and Wilson, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a claim about eusociality supported by citations.

claims.claim: Group selection may be important for the evolution of multicellularity from aggregations of single-celled organisms.
claims.source: Group level birth and death events, and hence group selection, may also be very important for the evolution of multicellularity from aggregations of single-celled organisms (Hammerschmidt et al., 2014; Ratcliff et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a claim about multicellularity evolution supported by citations.

claims.claim: Cultural evolution refers to the waxing and waning of ideas and cultural practices throughout human history.
claims.source: Cultural evolution refers to the waxing and waning of ideas and cultural practices throughout the history of human societies.
claims.evidence: This is a definition of cultural evolution.

claims.claim: Cultural evolution is a powerful alternative to genetic evolution that shapes many aspects of human life.
claims.source: Cultural evolution is a powerful alternative to genetic evolution that shapes a myriad of aspects of human life, from tool making to music and religion (Boyd and Richerson, 1985; Richerson and Boyd, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of cultural evolution supported by citations.

claims.claim: Cultural evolution is non-genetic but is thought to interact with human genetics in gene-culture coevolution.
claims.source: Cultural evolution is non-genetic, but is often thought to interact with human genetics, leading to gene-culture coevolution (Laland et al., 2010), in which cultural practices may generate selection pressures for certain genetic changes (such as the ability to adhere to norms (Chudek and Henrich, 2011), and genetic predispositions (e.g. in terms of brain function) determine constraints on cultural evolution.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of gene-culture coevolution supported by citations.

claims.claim: Much of cultural evolution must be non-genetic as evidenced by enormous cultural changes in the last 100 or 1000 years.
claims.source: That much of cultural evolution must be non-genetic is evident from the enormous cultural and societal changes in the last 100 or 1000 years.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on historical observation.

claims.claim: Models of cultural evolution most often closely resemble population genetic models of human evolution.
claims.source: Even though cultural evolution is non-genetic, models of cultural evolution nevertheless most often closely resemble population genetic models of human evolution (Mesoudi et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is an observation about modeling approaches supported by citation.

claims.claim: An alternative approach to modeling cultural evolution is to consider cultural ideas as reproductive units themselves.
claims.source: An alternative way to model cultural evolution consists of considering cultural ideas as reproductive units themselves, so that the evolutionary birth-death process is defined at the level of cultural content.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical proposal for modeling cultural evolution.

claims.claim: Cultural units can be envisaged as colonizing human brains, much like microbes colonize the human gut.
claims.source: Once the units are defined, one can envisage them as colonizing human brains, much like microbes colonize and inhabit the human gut.
claims.evidence: This is an analogy proposed for understanding cultural evolution.

claims.claim: Cultural units may accumulate or vanish within individual brains, corresponding to birth and death.
claims.source: Thus, cultural units live in human habitats (brains), in which they may accumulate or vanish, corresponding to birth and death. For example, an individual brain might acquire a strong belief and later become agnostic again, corresponding to the waxing and waning of a population of cultural units within that brain.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical proposal for how cultural birth-death processes work.

claims.claim: Cultural units may be transmitted between brains through mechanisms such as conversations, reading, or social media.
claims.source: Also, cultural units may be transmitted between habitats (brains) through various mechanisms such as conversations, reading, or social media.
claims.evidence: This is based on knowledge of how cultural information spreads.

claims.claim: The approach of considering culture as reproductive units has been used to investigate constraints on cumulative cultural evolution.
claims.source: The approach of considering culture as the reproductive units in an evolutionary process has for example been used in Mesoudi (2011) to investigate constraints on cumulative cultural evolution, and in (Doebeli, 2011; Doebeli and Ispolatov, 2010b) in a model for diversification of religions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Organismic evolution in the biosphere is ultimately the consequence of some organisms dying and others giving birth.
claims.source: Organismic evolution in the biosphere is ultimately the consequence of some organisms dying and others giving birth to new organisms.
claims.evidence: This is a foundational claim based on biological knowledge.

claims.claim: Evolutionary birth-death processes are a natural starting point for both verbal and mathematical descriptions of evolution.
claims.source: Therefore, evolutionary birth-death processes are a natural starting point for both verbal and mathematical descriptions of evolution.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion from the foundational claim about birth and death.

claims.claim: The state space of an evolving system includes the space of all possible types, all possible type distributions, and environmental states.
claims.source: The state space of an evolving system is generally complicated and includes not only the space of all possible types (e.g. genotypes or phenotypes), but also all possible states of evolving populations (i.e., type distributions), as well as environmental states.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical characterization of the complexity of evolutionary systems.

claims.claim: The dynamics of evolutionary birth-death processes can be very complicated because birth and death rates are functions of the evolving system state.
claims.source: Because birth and death rates in an evolutionary birth-death process are functions of the state of the evolving system, which in turn changes due to to birth and death events, the dynamics of such processes can be very complicated (as illustrated in Videos 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim illustrated by the videos.

claims.claim: Deriving a general analytical theory of evolutionary birth-death processes is difficult, although substantial progress has been made.
claims.source: This implies that deriving a general analytical theory of evolutionary birth-death processes is difficult, although substantial progress has been made (e.g. Champagnat et al., 2006; 2008, Dieckmann and Law, 1996; Puhalskii and Simon, 2012; Simon, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field supported by citations.

claims.claim: Simplified descriptions of evolutionary birth-death processes can only be obtained by making significant assumptions.
claims.source: It also implies that simplified descriptions can only be obtained by making significant assumptions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the requirements for analytical tractability.

claims.claim: Finding a fitness function that predicts evolutionary outcomes as equilibria at fitness maxima is generally impossible for evolutionary birth-death processes.
claims.source: In particular, finding a "fitness" function that would predict the outcome of the evolutionary process as equilibria located at maxima of the fitness function is in general impossible.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the limitations of fitness-based approaches.

claims.claim: Situations in which constant fitness landscapes are a useful metaphor may be exceedingly rare.
claims.source: In fact, situations in which constant fitness landscapes are a useful metaphor may be exceedingly rare.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about the applicability of fitness landscapes.

claims.claim: Many empirical theories in physical sciences were introduced in the 19th century based on experimental data and mathematical tools.
claims.source: Many empirical theories were introduced in the physical sciences in the 19th century based on a wealth of experimental data and the development of appropriate mathematical tools. Examples include Ohm's law linking electrical current and resistivity, the Navier-Stokes equations describing flow of liquids and gases, the Mass Action law for chemical kinetics, or the heat conduction equation for the diffusive transport of heat and matter.
claims.evidence: This is historical knowledge about the development of physical theories.

claims.claim: Empirical theories in physics were later re-derived from microscopic descriptions in the 20th century.
claims.source: With advances in understanding the molecular nature of matter in the 20th century, such theories were later "re-derived" from newly discovered microscopic descriptions in a mathematically strict way as a "coarse-grained" limit for the time evolution of average fluxes and rates in macroscopic systems.
claims.evidence: This is historical knowledge about the development of statistical mechanics.

claims.claim: Microscopic re-derivations of empirical equations allowed delineation of the validity of coarse-grained theories.
claims.source: Such microscopic re-derivations of initially empirical and phenomenological equations allowed to delineate the validity of the coarse-grained theories by revealing the conditions for their applicability, which is usually restricted to systems where the number of particles is sufficiently large, and when systems are not too far from equilibrium.
claims.evidence: This is knowledge about the relationship between microscopic and macroscopic theories in physics.

claims.claim: Quantitative laws of evolution based on fitness notions are difficult to verify empirically due to experimental difficulties.
claims.source: But due to the formidable experimental difficulties, quantitative laws of evolution based on such notions are difficult to verify empirically.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the challenges in evolutionary biology.

claims.claim: It has been understood from the beginning that evolution is based on birth and death events of individual organisms.
claims.source: On the other hand, unlike in the case of the molecular nature of the macroscopic laws in physics and chemistry, it has been understood from the very beginning, at least implicitly, that evolution is based on the "microscopic" events of birth and death of individual organisms.
claims.evidence: This is a historical observation about evolutionary thinking.

claims.claim: Fisher's fundamental theorem of natural selection is essentially a bookkeeping equation based on given birth and death events.
claims.source: Indeed, corresponding microscopic theories have been developed early on, such as Fisher's "fundamental theorem of natural selection" (Fisher, 1930), which is essentially a bookkeeping equation based on given birth and death events.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of Fisher's theorem supported by citation.

claims.claim: Macroscopic notions of fitness have continued to dominate evolutionary descriptions due to their intuitive appeal and mathematical simplicity.
claims.source: Nevertheless, "macroscopic" notions of fitness have continued to dominate both the narrative and the quantitative description of evolution, probably due to their apparent intuitive appeal and obvious mathematical simplicity.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the persistence of fitness-based thinking.

claims.claim: The concept of fitness has played a major role in the development of evolutionary theory and has been very useful.
claims.source: The concept of fitness has of course played a major role in the the development of evolutionary theory, and as such has been very useful, and very widely used, albeit often without empirical or "microscopic" justification.
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the historical importance of fitness.

claims.claim: General conditions under which a fitness measure can be found that is optimized by evolution require very special assumptions.
claims.source: General conditions under which a fitness measure can be found that is optimized by an underlying evolutionary process have been studied by (Metz and Geritz, 2016; Metz et al., 2008), whose results confirm that the existence of a constant fitness function that would capture the evolutionary dynamics requires very special assumptions.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical result supported by citations.

claims.claim: Invasion fitness is the only general, model-independent fitness definition that can provide an explicit link between ecological and evolutionary dynamics.
claims.source: Because it is derived from underlying birth-death processes, invasion fitness is an intrinsically ecological quantity, and it appears to be the only general, i.e., model-independent fitness definition that can provide an explicit link between ecological and evolutionary dynamics.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the unique status of invasion fitness.

claims.claim: The perspective of evolution as a birth-death process is applicable to any problem in evolutionary biology.
claims.source: The perspective of evolution as a birth-death process is straightforward and is applicable to any problem in evolutionary biology.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the generality of the proposed framework.

claims.claim: Long-term evolutionary dynamics must ultimately be the consequence of evolutionary birth-death processes.
claims.source: In particular, long-term evolutionary dynamics must ultimately be the consequence of evolutionary birth-death processes, and models linking short-term ecological events to long-term macroevolutionary patterns have recently emerged (Doebeli and Ispolatov, 2017; Gascuel et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to recent work.

claims.claim: Long-term evolutionary dynamics are often likely to be complicated because the functions determining birth and death rates are non-linear and complicated.
claims.source: The functions determining birth and death rates in evolutionary birth-death processes are generally non-linear and complicated. As a consequence, long-term evolutionary dynamics are often likely to be complicated as well.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the implications of complex rate functions.

claims.claim: Evolutionary dynamics are particularly likely to be complicated if they unfold in high-dimensional type spaces.
claims.source: This is particularly true if evolutionary processes unfold in type spaces that are themselves complicated (e.g., high-dimensional, (Doebeli and Ispolatov, 2010a, 2014, 2017)
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to the authors' work.

claims.claim: Understanding the evolution of genotypic and phenotypic complexity is a central problem in evolutionary biology.
claims.source: which in turn highlights the central problem of understanding the evolution of genotypic and phenotypic complexity.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of an important problem in the field.

claims.claim: Adopting the perspective of evolutionary birth-death processes will be useful for obtaining satisfactory explanations for core problems in evolutionary biology.
claims.source: To obtain satisfactory explanations for this and other core problems in evolutionary biology, it will be useful to adopt the perspective of evolutionary birth-death processes.
claims.evidence: This is a concluding recommendation based on the arguments presented.

results.result: The authors propose a mechanistic framework for evolutionary theory based on individual organisms undergoing birth and death events at rates that depend on individual properties, population composition, and environmental conditions. This birth-death process is characterized as a Markov process that can be simulated using established computational methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C12 collectively establish the theoretical foundation of the birth-death framework. The framework is grounded in established biological knowledge (C7-C10), mathematical theory (C11), and computational methods (C12). The proposal is logically coherent and builds on well-established principles from stochastic processes and population biology.

results.result: The authors demonstrate through computational simulations (Videos 1 and 2, Figure 1) that evolutionary birth-death processes can exhibit non-equilibrium dynamics including cyclic and chaotic behavior in 2D and 3D phenotype spaces, contradicting the traditional view of evolution converging to fitness optima.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 and C67 are directly supported by the provided videos and Figure 1, which show cyclic dynamics in 2D space and chaotic dynamics in 3D space. The simulations provide concrete examples of complex evolutionary dynamics that do not converge to equilibria, supporting the authors' theoretical arguments about the limitations of constant fitness landscapes.

results.result: The authors argue that fitness is not a fundamental driver of evolution but rather a derived property that may not exist for general evolutionary birth-death processes. They draw an analogy to Lyapunov functions in dynamical systems theory, noting that most complex dynamical systems lack such functions, and similarly, most evolutionary processes should not be expected to have global, time-independent fitness functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C28, C45-C52 form a logically coherent argument connecting dynamical systems theory (C46-C47, supported by citation) to evolutionary biology. The inference that evolutionary birth-death processes generally lack global fitness functions (C49) follows logically from the established mathematical knowledge about Lyapunov functions and the complexity of birth-death processes. The conclusion that fitness is derived rather than fundamental (C50-C51) is a reasonable inference from this argument.

results.result: The authors characterize mainstream evolutionary thinking as dominated by the fitness landscape metaphor, where evolution is viewed as an optimization process converging to fitness maxima. They argue that scenarios with constant fitness landscapes are not generic and should be the exception rather than the norm.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C39 accurately characterize the fitness landscape concept in evolutionary biology, supported by appropriate citations (C35). The observation about units not being specified (C36) and assumptions about time-constancy (C37) are reasonable characterizations of common practice. The conclusion that constant fitness landscapes are exceptional (C44) follows logically from the complexity arguments developed elsewhere in the manuscript.

results.result: The authors present invasion fitness as a derived quantity from birth-death processes that defines a dynamical system on fitness landscapes. Unlike constant fitness landscapes, invasion fitness changes as evolution unfolds and can lead to counterintuitive outcomes such as populations evolving to occupy fitness minima. Invasion fitness is characterized as the only general, model-independent fitness definition linking ecological and evolutionary dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C71, C80, and C136 are well-supported by citations to adaptive dynamics literature (Champagnat, Dieckmann and Law, Geritz et al.). The mathematical framework (C64, C66) is established theory. The characterization of invasion fitness as ecological (C80) and its unique status (C136) are reasonable inferences from the theoretical framework. The claim about populations evolving to fitness minima (C71) is supported by citation to Geritz et al. (1998).

results.result: The authors argue that there is no fundamental distinction between ecological and evolutionary processes, as both are birth-death processes differing only in the offspring function. The distinction becomes one of time scales when offspring functions are close to identity, though this separation may break down when evolutionary innovations are large and frequent.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C83 form a coherent argument about the relationship between ecology and evolution. The inference that both are fundamentally birth-death processes (C77) follows logically from the framework. The time scale argument (C79, C81) is a reasonable inference, and the caveat about breakdown of time scale separation (C82-C83) appropriately acknowledges limitations, with microbes given as a plausible example.

results.result: The authors apply the birth-death framework to social evolution, arguing that social evolution emerges from individual birth and death rates rather than from individuals maximizing inclusive fitness. They contend that inclusive fitness, if derivable at all, would be a derived property rather than a fundamental ingredient, and that no fitness concept is fundamentally necessary for understanding social evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C95 apply the birth-death framework consistently to social evolution. The argument that individuals don't 'know' about inclusive fitness (C89) and that rates are calculated independently (C90) follows from the mechanistic nature of the framework. The claim that inclusive fitness is derived rather than fundamental (C92) is consistent with the general argument about fitness. The acknowledgment that many processes may be too complex for fitness measures (C94) appropriately recognizes limitations.

results.result: The authors critique the use of the Price equation for multi-level selection, arguing it is a data visualization tool operating at the individual level rather than a true multi-level model. They propose that genuine multi-level selection requires birth-death processes at multiple levels of biological organization, with group-level events such as fission and extinction.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C106 present a coherent critique of the Price equation (C97-C99, supported by citations) and a clear definition of multi-level selection in the birth-death framework (C100-C102). The citation to the authors' previous work (C103) provides support for the feasibility of multi-level birth-death models. The distinction between spatial clustering and true group selection (C106) is a reasonable inference from the requirement for group-level reproductive units.

results.result: The authors propose an alternative approach to modeling cultural evolution by treating cultural ideas themselves as reproductive units undergoing birth-death processes within and between human brains, analogous to microbes colonizing the human gut. This approach has been applied to study cumulative cultural evolution and religious diversification.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C118 present a speculative theoretical proposal (C114-C117 are marked as speculation or based on analogy). While the approach is conceptually interesting and has been applied in cited work (C118), the proposal lacks empirical validation or detailed theoretical development in this manuscript. The analogy to microbial colonization (C115) is creative but remains largely metaphorical without concrete operationalization.

results.result: The authors discuss the mathematical tractability of birth-death processes, noting that while the theory of stochastic processes is well-developed and any birth-death process can be described by a Master equation, analytical solutions are only possible for simple cases. Different approximations can describe the same process depending on the limits taken.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C63 accurately characterize the state of mathematical theory for stochastic processes, supported by appropriate citations (Karlin and Taylor, Van Kampen, Champagnat et al.). The limitations on analytical tractability (C58, C60) are well-established mathematical facts. The observation about different approximations (C62-C63) is supported by citations and represents a reasonable characterization of the mathematical landscape.

results.result: The authors note that evolutionary game theory, while powerful and insightful, is generally based on ad hoc fitness functions (such as payoff matrices) that are usually not derived from underlying birth-death processes, with few exceptions.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 provide a fair characterization of evolutionary game theory, supported by appropriate citations. The acknowledgment of the field's contributions (C54) balanced with the critique about ad hoc fitness functions (C55) is reasonable. The citation of exceptions (Traulsen et al., Huang et al.) demonstrates awareness of work that does derive game dynamics from stochastic processes.

results.result: The authors draw an analogy between the historical development of physics (where macroscopic theories were later re-derived from microscopic descriptions) and evolutionary biology, noting that while evolution has always been understood to involve birth and death events, macroscopic fitness concepts have dominated due to their intuitive appeal and mathematical simplicity, despite often lacking microscopic justification.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C135 present a reasonable historical analogy supported by general knowledge of physics history (C127-C129) and evolutionary biology (C131-C134). The characterization of Fisher's theorem (C132) is supported by citation. The speculation about why fitness concepts persist (C133) is plausible. The citation to Metz and Geritz (C135) provides support for the claim that constant fitness functions require special assumptions.

results.result: The authors characterize the common definition of evolution and note its tautological aspects, drawing an analogy to how statistical physics provides a more mechanistic understanding of temperature and heat transfer as emergent properties of molecular interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 accurately represent standard definitions and critiques in evolutionary biology, supported by appropriate citations (Lewontin 1970, Ariew and Lewontin 2004, Dawkins 1982). The analogy to statistical physics (C4) is appropriate and helps motivate the mechanistic approach. These claims provide necessary context for the main argument.

results.result: The authors argue that evolutionary dynamics should be expected to be complicated when unfolding in high-dimensional type spaces, based on their previous work showing that complexity is generic in such scenarios.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C139-C140 are supported by citations to the authors' previous work (Doebeli and Ispolatov 2010a, 2014, 2017; Ispolatov et al. 2016). While the claim about 'most' dynamics being complicated (C43) is strong, it is presented as the authors' argument supported by their published work. The inference about complexity from non-linear rate functions (C139) is reasonable.

results.result: The authors suggest that group selection may be important for the evolution of eusociality and multicellularity from single-celled aggregations.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 are speculative (marked as speculation in evidence_type) and supported only by citations to other work rather than analysis or data in this manuscript. While the citations provide some support, these claims represent applications of the framework rather than results demonstrated in this paper. The modal verb 'may' appropriately indicates uncertainty.

results.result: The authors note that the birth-death framework can be extended to include additional events like dispersal or physiological state changes, and that in some organisms like fungi or plants, biomass growth may substitute for reproduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 describe reasonable extensions and modifications of the framework. These are presented as possibilities (C23 uses 'can be augmented', C24 uses 'may be') rather than definitive claims. The suggestion about biomass growth (C24) is based on biological knowledge about these organisms and represents a reasonable adaptation of the framework.

results.result: The authors provide background on cultural evolution, defining it as the dynamics of ideas and cultural practices, noting it is non-genetic but may interact with genetics in gene-culture coevolution, and observing that cultural evolution models typically resemble population genetic models.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C113 provide accurate background on cultural evolution, supported by appropriate citations (Boyd and Richerson, Laland et al., Mesoudi et al.). The inference that cultural evolution must be largely non-genetic based on rapid historical changes (C112) is reasonable. These claims provide necessary context for the subsequent application of the birth-death framework to cultural evolution.

results.result: The authors conclude that evolutionary birth-death processes are a natural starting point for evolutionary theory, that the dynamics can be very complicated, that deriving general analytical theory is difficult, and that finding global fitness functions is generally impossible. They argue this perspective is applicable to any problem in evolutionary biology and will be useful for addressing core problems like the evolution of complexity.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C126 and C137-C142 form the concluding synthesis of the manuscript. The foundational claim (C119-C120) follows logically from biological first principles. The characterization of complexity (C121-C122) is supported by the videos. The claims about mathematical difficulty (C123-C124) are supported by citations. The claims about applicability (C137) and usefulness (C142) are reasonable inferences from the arguments presented, though somewhat speculative about future utility.
